lines: Five tests passed. The code did nothing.
If an AI writes your code and your tests in one go, this can happen to you. Both come from the same guess about your data, so they agree with each other, even when the guess is wrong.

Here's a real one. A script was meant to log what every AI job cost. It looked for a field called role at the top of each record. The real records keep role one level down, inside message. So it matched nothing, wrote nothing, and exited clean.
Its five tests used sample records in the same flat shape the code expected. So all five passed.
One real record, run through it: zero lines.
So before you trust the green, give your AI one real example. A real log, a real API response, a real file. Have it build a test from that. Your tests should start from your data, not from the guess.
facts: Draft 2 script (Robin's notes on draft 1, 2026-10-31: too abstract, 'made up' lost him, the video must relate to something viewers actually do). Every claim about the bug is from devweb.org/articles/agent-run-cost-attribution (devweb content/articles/agent-run-cost-attribution.mdx), section 'Five tests passed. The hook wrote nothing.' I: the section title. II: advice to the viewer, generalising the article's 'Any time you build a fixture from the same document that guided the implementation, the fixture and the code can be wrong together and agree with each other forever' and 'A schema you read once and encoded in both places is a single point of failure'. The article does not say an AI wrote these fixtures, so the script does not claim it. III: the hook reads each finished agent's transcript and appends its token usage to the run's log (cost attribution, SPAWN-TOKEN-EVENT); 'The selector read .role == "user"'; 'Real ... transcripts don't put role at the top level' ({"type":"user","message":{"role":"user",...}}); 'The selector matched zero lines ... it exited 0 and wrote nothing.' IV: 'The hook had five test fixtures, and all five passed ... every one had synthesized its user lines in the flat shape the hook expected.' V: 'When someone finally ran a real subagent transcript through the hook and counted the SPAWN-TOKEN-EVENT lines, the count was zero.' VI: 'It's feeding the thing a real input'; 'an end-to-end proof fixture: feed the hook a real-schema transcript'; 'The only fixture that breaks the tie is one whose input you didn't invent.' On screen: the receipt 'job 1 · 84,749 tokens' is the article's example SPAWN-TOKEN-EVENT (processed 84749). Product names left out.
